name: IT CAME UPON A MIDNIGHT GRUYERE BURGER

recipe.history:
Gruyère is Switzerland's most celebrated cheese, a wheel of raw cow's milk aged in the caves and cellars of the Fribourg region — specifically in and around the town of Gruyères, from which it takes its name — for a minimum of five months and often for twelve, eighteen, or even twenty-four months for premium grades. Its production is documented as far back as the twelfth century, when alpine herders developed the technology of pressing large wheels of cooked curd as a way to preserve summer milk through the long mountain winter. The characteristic small eyes, the smooth pale ivory paste, the flavor that moves from mild and milky in young wheels to deeply nutty, complex, and faintly crystalline in aged ones — all of these are the product of centuries of accumulated knowledge, specific alpine bacteria, the particular grasses of Swiss mountain pastures, and the patient application of time. Gruyère received AOC protection in 2001 and AOP status in 2013, meaning that true Gruyère can only come from its defined geographical region and must be made according to strict traditional methods. It is, by almost any measure, one of the greatest melting cheeses in existence: its fat content and protein structure allow it to flow into a smooth, bubbling pool under heat without breaking or becoming greasy, a quality that made it the definitive choice for fondue and French onion soup.

Gruyère's appearance on American burgers is inseparable from the French onion soup tradition. Gratinéed onion soup — rich beef broth, wine-braised onions, a crouton, and a molten cap of Gruyère — became a staple of French-American restaurants in the 1960s and 1970s, introduced to mainstream American diners by the wave of French culinary enthusiasm that followed Julia Child's influence. Ambitious burger restaurants of the 1990s and 2000s began translating the components of French onion soup onto a patty: caramelized onions, a splash of beef stock, a generous blanket of Gruyère — creating a burger that tasted like everything that was right about both traditions at once. The beef of the burger and the beef of the broth, the sweetness of the onions, the nutty melt of the cheese — it is a combination that seems both inevitable and slightly miraculous.

I first made a French onion burger on a winter night when I had been making soup all day and the house smelled of long-cooked onions and wine and beef stock. I had extra caramelized onions and extra Gruyère and a pound of ground beef in the refrigerator, and the burger practically assembled itself. The moment the cheese melted over the onions and the patty, and I bit through the toasted bun into that combination of sweet and nutty and beefy and rich, I understood that I had stumbled onto something I could not un-taste. There is a particular comfort in French onion flavors — the sweetness of deeply caramelized onion, the complex nuttiness of aged Gruyère — that feels like being looked after. Putting that on a burger makes the burger feel like the best possible version of a winter evening.

Gruyère at medium rare is a different experience than Gruyère on a well-done patty, and the difference is not subtle. On a medium rare patty — one that rests between 130 and 135 degrees Fahrenheit — the cheese pools and trembles, its fat still liquid, mixing with the juices that seep from the meat below. On a well-done patty, the cheese sits on a dry surface and begins to congeal almost immediately, its fat separating from the protein in a way that is not pleasant to taste or to look at. The caramelized onions, with all their concentrated sweetness and moisture, deserve to sit on a patty that is still alive with its own moisture. Medium rare is what makes the three elements — beef, onions, Gruyère — become one thing rather than three things stacked on bread.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
For the French onion caramelized onions:
4 thick slices aged Gruyère (for direct melt on patty)
4 large leaves frisée or curly endive
instructions: 1. Caramelize the onions: Melt butter with olive oil in a large heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Add sliced onions, salt, and sugar. Cook, stirring every 8–10 minutes, for 50–60 minutes until deeply golden-brown and jammy throughout. Add white wine and increase heat to medium, stirring to deglaze. Add beef stock and thyme sprigs and cook until liquid is absorbed, about 10 more minutes. Add Worcestershire and black pepper, stir, and remove thyme. Set aside.

2. Make the Gruyère mornay: Melt butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in flour and cook 1–2 minutes until the roux smells nutty. Slowly whisk in milk and cream, adding in a thin stream. Cook, whisking constantly, until thickened and smooth, about 4–5 minutes. Remove from heat, add grated Gruyère, dry mustard, white pepper, and nutmeg. Stir until smooth and glossy. Season with salt. Keep warm over very low heat.

3. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
4. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.
5. Divide into 4 equal portions. Shape into smooth balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 45 minutes.
6. Brush buns with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

7. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions of about 170g each. Gently mix Worcestershire into meat. Form into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
9. Place a thick slice of Gruyère on each patty. Add a splash of water, cover immediately, and steam 30–45 seconds until cheese is melted and bubbling.
10. Transfer patties to a resting rack and rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
11. Reheat caramelized onions gently if needed. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

12. Assemble: Spread Dijon mustard on the top bun. Spread a spoonful of warm Gruyère mornay sauce on the bottom bun. Place frisée on the bottom bun. Set the cheesed patty on the frisée. Pile a generous mound of caramelized onions on the patty. Drizzle additional mornay sauce over the onions. Finish with flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately.
